summary: Registers a URN namespace with the identifier "ogc" for the Open Geospatial Consortium. The namespace is used to give persistent names to resources the OGC publishes, such as its technical specifications. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Names for things on the web can change. This paper gives a geography standards group a special name-tag style so its documents keep the same name forever.

subtitle: Permanent, location-independent names for geospatial resources.

tldr.problem: The Open Geospatial Consortium publishes standards and resources whose web locations can change over time, but the standards need stable, persistent identifiers for long-term reference.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5165 registers a URN namespace identifier "ogc" that allows the OGC to assign persistent, globally unique names to all its published resources following a standard format.
tldr.outcome: OGC resources now have stable identifiers that do not depend on where they are hosted on the web, making them reliable for long-term use in standards and software.

today: RFC 5165 remains the active standard for the OGC URN namespace. The namespace is registered with IANA and in active use by the geospatial community for persistent identification of standards, schemas, and coordinate reference systems.

sections.title: Names That Don't Break When Things Move
sections.content:
The Open Geospatial Consortium produces technical standards and specifications for managing spatial data and geospatial services. These specifications are referenced by other standards from OASIS, IETF, IEEE, and ISO.

The problem: if an OGC specification moves from one URL to another (due to website restructuring, server migration, or organizational change), every reference to it breaks. A Uniform Resource Name (URN) solves this by providing a persistent identifier that is independent of location, like an ISBN for a book.
sections.eli5: Standards are cited in other standards for decades. A stable name is more important than a stable website.

sections.title: URN Namespace Structure
sections.content:
A URN has the format urn:<namespace-id>:<namespace-specific-string>. The namespace ID "ogc" identifies resources managed by the Open Geospatial Consortium. The namespace-specific string follows a hierarchical structure: urn:ogc:{OGCresource}:{ResourceSpecificString}.

For example, urn:ogc:specification:gml:doc-is(02-023r4):3.0.0 uniquely identifies version 3.0.0 of an OGC specification document for Geography Markup Language (GML). The OGC Naming Authority (ONA) manages all assignments within this namespace.
sections.eli5: A URN is like a filing system: the first part says who manages it (OGC), and the rest describes exactly which resource and what version.

sections.title: OGC Namespace Registration Details
sections.content:
RFC 5165 registers the formal namespace identifier "ogc" with IANA (the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) under the URN registration process described in RFC 3406. The registration was completed on August 16, 2007.

The OGC Naming Authority (ONA) serves as the registrant and maintains a permanent registry of approved resource types and registrations. Entries in the registry are published on the OGC website and are structured so each resource class has its own description and registration table.

The namespace supports three types of registration activities: standard uses from OGC specifications, registration of sub-trees to other organizations, and experimental name models for testing.
sections.eli5: The OGC assigned someone to keep a permanent list of all the names they have handed out and what each one means.

sections.title: Examples of OGC URNs
sections.content:
The RFC provides three concrete examples:

Specification reference: urn:ogc:specification:gml:doc-is(02-023r4):3.0.0 identifies a specific version of GML in the OGC document archives.

Service type: urn:ogc:serviceType:CatalogueService:2.0.2:HTTP identifies an OGC catalog service type, allowing applications to specify which service they need.

Coordinate Reference System: urn:ogc:def:crs:EPSG:6.3:26986 references a specific coordinate system definition from the EPSG database, showing how URNs can identify precise technical definitions essential for geographic information systems.
sections.eli5: These examples show that the same URN system works for standards documents, service definitions, and technical data—anything the OGC publishes.

sections.title: Why the OGC Needs Its Own Namespace
sections.content:
The RFC explains that existing URN namespaces (such as those used by OASIS or OMA) do not fully support the semantics needed for geospatial content and services. Geospatial data has unique characteristics, such as the need to express coordinate reference systems and multi-dimensional spatial relationships, that require specialized naming capabilities.

Additionally, as OGC standards have been adopted by government agencies (NATO, NGA) and other standards organizations, the need for persistent, reliable resource identifiers has become critical. Agencies often mandate OGC standards compliance, making stable URNs essential for compliance verification and documentation.
sections.eli5: Geography has special technical needs that other standards bodies did not think about, so OGC needed its own naming system.

sections.title: Community Benefits and Openness
sections.content:
The URN namespace and the OGC Naming Authority are open community resources. Any person or organization can submit a proposal for new resources to the ONA, which processes requests through normal OGC standards discussion and approval procedures.

Since 2003, the OGC membership has developed expertise in using OGC URNs through implementation experiments and operational test beds. An OGC URN resolver operates at urn.opengis.net, and a public registry is maintained at www.opengeospatial.org/ogcna. This ensures that URNs remain freely and openly available for use by both OGC members and the broader IT community.
sections.eli5: Anyone can propose new URNs, and everyone can look up what existing ones mean through public registries and tools.

references.text: Daigle, L., van Gulik, D., Iannella, R., and P. Faltstrom, "Uniform Resource Names (URN) Namespace Definition Mechanisms", RFC 3406, October 2002.
